help.common.faq.data.q: Where is my data? Does anything leave my computer?
help.common.faq.data.a: Your review is the project JSON file on your own disk, next to its PDFs — the app has no account, no server, and no sync.
help.common.faq.concurrent.q: Can two people review the same project at once?
help.common.faq.concurrent.a: Not on the same copy at the same time — the app has no locking. When a save finds files that changed on disk since you opened the project, it stops and asks: keep your version, keep theirs, or combine the two field by field. Copies passed around by email or a folder that hasn't synced yet can still diverge. What it does support is multiple reviewers within one file: set the reviewer count when you build the schema, and each reviewer's answers are kept separately (see {reviewers}). Give each person their own git clone, or take turns.
help.common.faq.moved.q: I moved the JSON and now the PDFs don't load.
help.common.faq.moved.a: PDFs are referenced relative to the JSON file, so the PDFs need to travel with it. Moving the JSON with Save as… re-derives the references for you; moving it in Finder/Explorer does not. In the browser you'll also be asked once per session to point at the folder that holds them.
help.common.faq.consolidation.q: Why did my Findings get reordered — and why is my project suddenly unsaved?
help.common.faq.consolidation.a1: Opening a paper as Consolidation lines the reviewers up: it works out which of each reviewer's repeated entries are the same entry and puts them in the same order, so that everyone's Finding #2 means one finding. Without that, comparing #2 against #2 would pit unrelated findings against each other and report a disagreement that was really just a difference of ordering.
help.common.faq.consolidation.a2: Because that changes the file, it counts as an unsaved change — and it is a single Undo away if you would rather keep the original order. Your own values are never altered, only their order, and a gap can appear where you recorded nothing for an entry the others did. Once you have answered a group in Consolidation, it is left alone.
help.common.faq.autosave.a: No. A dot before the project name in the window title means unsaved changes — press {mod}+S. The app asks before you close or quit with unsaved work.
help.start.lead.1: SaiLoR supports Systematic Literature Reviews. Everything for a review lives in a single project JSON file, which holds two things: an annotation schema — the fields you want to extract from every paper — and the list of papers, each pointing at its PDF.
help.start.lead.2: While reviewing, the app shows the paper's PDF next to a form built from your schema. You fill the fields in (grabbing text straight from the PDF if you like), and the answers are saved back into the same JSON file — ready to hand to a co-reviewer or analyse later.
help.start.options.title: Your options from here
help.start.options.open: Open project… — open an existing project JSON and start annotating. If you've opened projects before, they're listed underneath for one click, each with a ✎ to jump straight into editing its schema.
help.start.options.new: New annotation JSON… — start a review from scratch. You choose where the JSON should live, define the annotation schema (the fields, their types, whether they repeat or nest), and attach the PDFs to review.
help.start.options.edit: Edit annotation JSON… — open an existing project and change its schema or its list of papers. Annotations already filled in are preserved.
help.start.which.title: Which one do I want?
help.start.which.text: If somebody handed you a project file, use Open project…. If you're setting up a new review, use New annotation JSON… — you can always come back and adjust the schema later with Edit annotation JSON….
help.start.faq.project.a: One JSON file. It carries the schema, the paper list, and every answer anybody has filled in. There is no database and no hidden state — copy that file (and its PDFs) and you have copied the whole review.
help.start.faq.handJson.q: Do I need to write JSON by hand?
help.start.faq.handJson.a: No. New annotation JSON… builds it for you. The format is documented if you want to hand-edit or generate it, and the app reads hand-edited files defensively — but nothing here requires it.
help.annotate.lead: You have a project open: read each paper's PDF in the middle and fill in the annotation fields on the right. Everything is saved back into the project JSON you opened.
help.annotate.workflow.title: Basic workflow
help.annotate.workflow.open: Open a project via the Open ▾ menu — pick a file or a recent project. To create or change a project's schema, use New annotation JSON… / Edit annotation JSON… on the start screen.
help.annotate.workflow.pick: Pick a paper from the left list — a project opens on the first paper you have not marked finished, so reopening a review lands where the work is. Each paper's dot fills as its fields are filled in — amber while it is still yours to finish, green once you tick Annotation finished at the top of the annotation panel, red if you tick it while fields are still empty. The dropdown under the search box filters the list by that state and counts it. The button in the list's header hides the list to make room for the paper; once hidden, the same button in the top bar brings it back.
help.annotate.workflow.read: Read the PDF in the middle pane; its text is selectable. Use {mod}+F to search within it. After following an internal link (e.g. a reference), the ↩ / ↪ buttons jump back to where you were and forward again. Hovering an internal link or a numbered citation such as [3] previews its target, also in PDFs whose citations are not clickable.
help.annotate.workflow.annotate: Annotate on the right. Repeatable entries show + Add and a remove (×) control. Use the ⧉ button next to a field to insert the text currently selected in the PDF.
help.annotate.workflow.info: A field name with a ⓘ next to it has a description — hover for a quick look, or right-click to keep it open: its text is selectable and any link in it is clickable, which the hover version can't offer since it closes as soon as the mouse moves toward it.
help.annotate.workflow.validate: Validate checks your annotations against the schema: required fields that are still empty, values of the wrong type, and values outside a dropdown's choices. Required fields are marked with a red *.
help.annotate.workflow.save: Save via the Save ▾ menu (or {mod}+S). "Save as…" writes to a new file, and the PDF references are re-derived so they still resolve from there.
help.annotate.searching.title: Finding a paper
help.annotate.searching.p1: The box above the paper list searches title, authors, and DOI — the META trigger inside its right-hand edge. Click it to switch to TAGS, which searches the annotation content you have already recorded instead — for answering "which papers did I mark as X". The trigger is highlighted while annotation search is on, so you can always tell which mode you are in.
help.annotate.searching.p2: Annotation search looks at the answers of whoever you are currently reviewing as, so in a multi-reviewer project it finds your work, not somebody else's.
help.annotate.reviewers.title: Working with several reviewers
help.annotate.reviewers.p1: A project can be set up so that several reviewers annotate it independently — the usual way to keep an SLR honest. If it is, the top bar lets you say who you are. Each reviewer sees and fills in only their own answers; nobody is influenced by what anyone else recorded.
help.annotate.reviewers.p2: Besides the numbered reviewers there is one extra role, Consolidation. That is not "one more reviewer" — it is the pass where the disagreements get settled. In Consolidation, each field gets a compare button that shows every reviewer's answer side by side, flags whether they agree, and lets you click one to adopt it. What Consolidation records is the project's final result — the answers an analysis or export would use.
help.annotate.reviewers.p3: Where every reviewer gave the same answer, Consolidation fills it in for you and marks it with a light-blue border until you click it — there is nothing to reconcile when everyone already agrees, and copying those across by hand is exactly the task during which a real disagreement further down gets missed. Only case and stray spaces are forgiven, never near-misses: if the wording genuinely differs, the call stays yours. A field one reviewer left blank is not agreement either, however the others answered.
help.annotate.reviewers.p4: For fields and groups that can be added several times — Findings, say — Consolidation does two things for you as you open a paper. It adds as many entries as the busiest reviewer recorded, so you are not counting anyone's work by hand. And it works out which of each reviewer's entries are the same entry, since two people listing the same three findings rarely list them in the same order. Your Finding #2 is then everyone's Finding #2, and the compare button lines up answers that are genuinely about the same thing instead of reporting a disagreement that was only a difference of ordering. Entries are matched on what they say, so wording need not match exactly; once you have answered a group, it is left alone rather than re-ordered underneath you.
help.annotate.reviewers.p5: Two buttons above the annotation fields belong to Consolidation. ⚠ Disagreements lists every field the reviewers answered differently across the whole project — click one to jump straight to it, rather than hunting paper by paper. ⚖ Agreement reports the usual inter-rater coefficients — Cohen's κ, Fleiss' κ and Krippendorff's α — and you can tick any combination. One that cannot honestly be computed for your project is greyed out and tells you why when you hover it, rather than quietly reporting a number that would not mean what it appears to.
help.annotate.reviewers.p6: Two reviewers can write RCT and randomized controlled trial and mean one thing, which no amount of text comparison can know. When you see such a pair in the compare popup, tick "These answers mean the same thing": from then on the app counts it as agreement — in the badge, in the disagreement list, and in the statistics. It is worth doing before you quote a κ anywhere, because until you do, the number understates how much your reviewers actually agreed.
help.annotate.reviewers.p7: Ticking it settles that they agreed, not what they agreed on, so also click one of the answers to record the value. If you try to leave without doing that, the app stops and asks: the field would otherwise count as settled while holding nothing, and you would never see it again. Leave anyway and the tick is undone, so the field goes back on the disagreement list rather than quietly vanishing from it.
help.annotate.reviewers.p8: Opening such a project asks who you are before showing you anything — an answer that isn't attributable to a reviewer is worse than no answer. It asks once, and each paper then remembers the seat you last read it in, so you can be Reviewer 1 on some papers and Reviewer 2 on others; the toolbar switch changes it whenever you like. With git, a notice warns you when someone else has already committed your seat on the paper you're on.
help.annotate.reviewers.p9: You don't have to wait for everyone to finish before consolidating: the seat is always open, and it is the individual papers that wait. One that not every reviewer has annotated yet keeps its ⇄ buttons disabled and says so in its dot's tooltip — the missing reviewer's column would otherwise look like they found nothing, when the truth is they haven't looked yet. The line under Papers counts those, as the … · 3/10 ready half of its text.
help.annotate.reviewers.p10: Consolidation signs papers off like any other seat: the checkbox at the top of the panel reads Consolidation finished, the paper's dot fills as the consolidated record fills and turns green once you tick it, and the filter dropdown narrows the list to what you have not settled yet. That tick is yours alone — it is stored with the consolidated result and claims nothing about whether the reviewers have all answered the paper.
help.annotate.faq.validate.q: Validate says nothing is wrong, but I know papers are empty.
help.annotate.faq.validate.a: Papers with no annotations at all are skipped rather than reported — an untouched paper would otherwise fail every required field at once and bury the real problems. They are listed separately, under Not annotated yet, so you can still see them.
help.annotate.faq.yesNo.q: Why isn't my required Yes/no field flagged as missing?
help.annotate.faq.yesNo.a: A Yes/no field always counts as answered: an unticked box is a real answer (no), and the file cannot tell "not answered" apart from "answered no". If you need a true third state, use a Text field with fixed choices instead.
help.annotate.faq.schema.q: Can I change the schema after people have annotated?
help.annotate.faq.schema.a: Yes — Edit annotation JSON… on the start screen. Existing answers are preserved. Renaming or moving a field takes its answers along when you save, unless you choose to keep them hidden; removing one hides them from every screen and export, and they come back if the field does.
help.screening.lead: This project screens papers rather than annotating them: one Include / Exclude decision per paper, made fast, usually from the title and abstract alone.
help.screening.what.title: What screening is
help.screening.what.p: A screening project has no authored schema — every screening project records exactly the same thing: a decision and, when excluded, a reason. It is the first pass of a systematic review: hundreds of records, seconds each, deciding which survive into the annotation phase that follows.
help.screening.decision.title: Why a dropdown, not a checkbox
help.screening.decision.p: The decision is Include / Exclude, not a single "Exclude" checkbox, because the app has to be able to say "not screened yet" — a state a checkbox cannot hold. Every boolean field in this app reads an unticked box as a real, deliberate "no", so a checkbox could never tell "I decided to include this" apart from "I haven't looked yet". Progress, the PRISMA counts, and which papers an import carries forward all depend on that distinction.
help.screening.reasons.title: Why the reason list is fixed
help.screening.reasons.p: The exclusion reasons are set once, before screening starts, by whoever built the project — the same way a review protocol pre-registers its exclusion criteria. That is what makes the ◧ Summary's per-reason counts meaningful: free text would let every reviewer phrase the same reason differently, and the counts (and the PRISMA flow diagram they feed) would not add up to anything.
help.screening.keys.title: The fast keyboard flow
help.screening.keys.p: Press <kbd>I</kbd> to include or <kbd>E</kbd> to exclude the paper on screen; <kbd>U</kbd> undoes a decision back to "not screened". Deciding a paper for the first time automatically moves to the next undecided one, so screening a stack is a rhythm of read-decide-read rather than read-decide-click-next; going back to fix an earlier call never jumps you away again. A digit <kbd>1</kbd>–<kbd>9</kbd> excludes with the corresponding configured reason (in the order the project lists them) in one press.
help.screening.reviewers.title: Several reviewers, and Consolidation
help.screening.reviewers.p: Screening reuses the same reviewer/Consolidation machinery every other part of this app does: two reviewers screen independently, and Consolidation reconciles them into the final decision — the standard SLR screening protocol. Where every reviewer decided the same way, Consolidation can adopt all of those decisions at once with Adopt all, and ⚖ Agreement reports Cohen's/Fleiss' κ over the include/exclude decision specifically — the statistic a screening phase actually reports, and the reason this reuses the consolidation machinery rather than building something parallel to it.
help.screening.ai.title: AI proposals
help.screening.ai.p: AI can propose Include/Exclude decisions (with a reason and a quote from the abstract) for the current paper or all undecided ones, judged against the project's protocol. Titles and abstracts are sent to your chosen provider. Nothing is written until you tick rows and press Apply; Exclude proposals never start ticked, and papers you have already decided are never overwritten.
help.screening.summary.title: The summary and PRISMA
help.screening.summary.p: ◧ Summary shows progress and the include / exclude / undecided totals, plus how many papers were excluded for each configured reason — the numbers a PRISMA flow diagram reports. It states which seat it is counting (your own decisions, or the consolidated result), since the two can differ.
help.screening.importing.title: Starting an annotation project from this one
help.screening.importing.p: Once screening is done, use New from screening… (on the start screen) to build the next-phase annotation project: every paper not explicitly excluded is carried over — included papers always, and undecided ones by default, since dropping a paper nobody actually excluded would silently shrink the review. The new project is saved next to this screening JSON by default, so relative PDF paths keep resolving unchanged.
help.editor.lead: This is where you define a project: the annotation schema (the fields reviewers fill in for every paper) and the PDFs to annotate. It writes the project JSON that the annotation view then opens.
help.editor.location.title: Where the JSON lives
help.editor.location.p: The location is chosen up front and shown at the top — use Change… to move it. PDFs are referenced relative to the JSON file, so if you move the JSON the references are re-derived for you.
help.editor.schema.title: Building the schema
help.editor.schema.add: Add a field with + Add field, or nest one under another with + Child. Each field has a name, a type, and an optional description shown on hover while annotating — right-click it there to keep it open with any link in it clickable.
help.editor.schema.type: Type: Text, Number, Yes/no, or Group — a group holds no value of its own and just contains nested fields.
help.editor.schema.repeats: Repeats: min and max control how many times a field can occur. Tick ∞ for an unbounded number — the annotator then gets + Add to create as many entries as needed.
help.editor.schema.choices: Fixed choices: on a Text field, add options to turn it into a dropdown. With no options it stays free text.
help.editor.schema.reorder: Reorder and nest by dragging a row's ⠿ handle: drop near a row's top or bottom edge to place it before or after, or drop in the middle of a row to nest it inside that row.
help.editor.reviewers.title: Setting up several reviewers
help.editor.reviewers.p: Turn on multiple reviewers and give a count to have the project annotated independently by that many people — each sees only their own answers. On top of the number you choose, the project always gets one extra Consolidation role: whoever takes it compares everyone's answers field by field and records the final, agreed result, which is what the project's output actually contains. So "2 reviewers" means two independent passes plus a consolidation pass.
help.editor.ai.title: AI-assisted annotation
help.editor.ai.p: The AI toolbar button sends a paper's content to a configured AI model and proposes values for its still-empty fields — nothing is written until you review and press Apply. Settings (the gear icon) is your model library: configure a provider, model, and key once. The setup screen then just assigns library models to roles — Annotator (required), Judge (agent mode) and Cross-check (optional) — remembered per project. Prompt mode is one request per paper; Agent mode lets the model search and re-read the paper with tools and adds a second-pass judge review, at considerably more cost and time; Classify mode asks a fast, very cheap System One decision model (a calibrated probability, no quotes) for yes/no and single-choice fields only. A System One model can also be assigned as a Cross-check in Prompt/Agent mode: it answers the same eligible fields independently, and a confident disagreement starts that row unticked for a closer look. Turning on "annotate all papers" runs every eligible paper instead of just the current one — several at once (configurable), with a spending cap, a Skip action per in-flight paper, and the option to resume a run that was cancelled, skipped, or stopped partway. A setup-screen toggle can also show the model your own already-finished papers as worked examples of the review's conventions. In the review table, Edit lets you correct a proposed value yourself before applying it — it's still recorded as AI-assisted, just with your value instead of the model's. Under Options, "re-check fields I've already filled" is optional (off each time) and never overwrites an answer unless you tick the proposed replacement; in Agent mode the model can optionally search the web through Anthropic or OpenRouter; and, in the desktop app, a summary of which fields the AI left empty, got flagged or that you corrected is saved to annotations/feedback/ in the project folder (field values only, no paper text) to help improve the schema. In the desktop app, Settings can also set up local models: chat models served by Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp or vLLM, and small System One decision models the app downloads and runs itself. Every download shows its size, source and license and starts only after you confirm; models use the GPU when one is supported and otherwise run on the CPU (slower), and the model's context size is set explicitly so long papers are not silently cut. Papers stay on your machine unless the server is on another host, which the dialog warns about.
help.editor.aiSeat.title: Giving the AI a reviewer seat
help.editor.aiSeat.p: With at least 2 reviewers and AI-assisted annotation allowed, one project setting dedicates the last reviewer seat to the AI. Its answers are written into that seat like any human reviewer's, and compared against the others in Consolidation the same way — nothing about Consolidation changes to accommodate it. A human can still open that seat to look at or correct the AI's work; the annotation panel notes when you're looking at it.
help.editor.papers.title: Adding papers
help.editor.papers.intro: There are three ways to get papers into a project, and they mix freely:
help.editor.papers.addPdfs: + Add PDFs… — pick one or more PDFs.
help.editor.papers.addFolder: + Add folder… — take every PDF in a folder at once, including sub-folders.
help.editor.papers.import: Import references… — read a BibTeX (.bib), RIS (.ris) or CSL-JSON export from a reference manager such as Zotero, Mendeley or JabRef. This brings in titles, authors and DOIs; you still attach the PDFs themselves.
help.editor.papers.duplicates: A paper already in the project is never added twice. Importing references matches against what is already there — by DOI, otherwise by title — and fills in the gaps of a matching paper instead of duplicating it.
help.editor.papers.guessed: Newly added papers are marked with a blue border, because their title and authors are a best-effort guess read out of the PDF or the reference file. Check them; the mark clears as soon as you click into the row. Every field stays editable, and rows can be dragged to reorder.
help.editor.saving.title: Saving
help.editor.saving.p: Save JSON writes the file and leaves you here to keep working. Save JSON & Begin Annotating writes it and opens it for review. Both check the project first and tell you what to fix if something is off.
help.editor.faq.noPdf.q: An imported reference has no PDF. Is that a problem?
help.editor.faq.noPdf.a: It is flagged, and you should fix it before annotating: a paper needs a PDF to review. Importing a bibliography only brings the metadata — attach the file with + Add PDFs… or by typing the path into the row.
help.editor.faq.badTitle.q: The title or authors came out wrong.
help.editor.faq.badTitle.a: They are extracted heuristically — from the PDF's own metadata and layout, or from the reference file — and papers vary wildly. That is exactly why new rows are marked for review. Just type over anything that is wrong; nothing is locked.
help.editor.faq.reuse.q: Can I reuse one schema across several reviews?
help.editor.faq.reuse.a: Yes — copy the project JSON, then use Edit annotation JSON… to swap the papers out. The schema and the paper list are independent parts of the same file.
help.editor.faq.rename.q: What happens to answers if I rename a field?
help.editor.faq.rename.a: The answers move to the new name when you save — including other reviewers' once their work arrives, since every file records the schema version it was written under. A note under the field lets you keep them hidden instead. Answers can't follow a field out of or into a repeated group; those stay hidden, and Validate lists them.

help.appearance.p: Toggle light/dark with the ☾/☀ button and scale the app text with the A− A A+ buttons. These affect the app only — the PDF paper stays white and normal-sized.

git.repoSetup.reason: Two of git's defaults work against annotation data. On Windows, git normally rewrites every line ending on checkout, which turns one reviewer's machine into a source of whole-file diffs and phantom conflicts for everyone. And git's own merge will combine two reviewers' answers into a file that is valid JSON but that neither of them wrote — SaiLoR never uses that result, but anyone merging in a terminal gets it silently.

llm.settings.title: AI models
llm.settings.browserWarnTitle: Running in the browser — your API key is not protected here.
llm.settings.browserKeyBody: The key is saved unencrypted in this browser's local storage, where any script on this page — and anyone with access to this machine's browser profile — can read it. On top of that, some providers refuse requests made directly from a web page, and a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoint usually will (it has no CORS headers for this origin). The desktop app is the supported path for AI annotation; use a throwaway or tightly scoped key if you continue here.
llm.settings.keyNotice: The API key is stored encrypted with your operating system's keychain, is held by the app's main process, and is never handed to the page that renders this dialog. It is spliced into a request only as it is sent to the provider.

llm.settings.stateBudgetHint: The paper state (title, abstract, extracted text) is truncated to fit this budget. Jev's own context is about 64k tokens; Laya is far smaller (English 512, multilingual up to 8192) — for those, only the title and abstract will fit.
